defer:url:6f0fb0223e38d4b7.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide

candidate.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
candidate.summary:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:

  • Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
  • Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
  • Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
  • Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
  • Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data.

That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year.

The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README.

I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:

Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty.

Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score

How this works, using service workers

Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.

The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML.

This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.

The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.

Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:

/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)

Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about?

The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.

Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.

The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.

Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.

(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)

I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:

This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!

Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite

I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite.

Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.

Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.

In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.

WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.

datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:

pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl

That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.

Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.

Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:

This should work for every other Python app, too

Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.

C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.

One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.

I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers

candidate.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
candidate.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

defer:url:21b086fc4d484154.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents

candidate.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
candidate.summary: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

published.sourceTitle: “Does Meta think we can’t read?” Meta abandons sketchy commercial terms update.
published.sourceText:
Meta won’t force Facebook page owners to allow AI training on linked content.
After weeks of backlash —and a failed attempt to quell it —Meta has indefinitely delayed plans to update its commercial terms and require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.
“We’re pausing the ‌changes ⁠as we continue to engage with stakeholders and ​take ​our ⁠time to get this right. ​In the ​meantime, ⁠our existing terms remain in ⁠effect,” a Meta spokesperson told Reuters.
Soon after Meta notified business account holders of the upcoming changes, legal experts warned Nieman Lab that the vague language could allow the company to ignore scraping preferences specified in robots.txt files and exhaustively crawl vast amounts of off-Facebook content for AI training. Since virtually every news publisher has a Facebook page, Nieman Lab sounded the alarm that Meta could potentially avoid millions in licensing fees if the TOS update happened as planned.
Ars broke down the changes after Meta announced them, noting that businesses—including news publishers involved in drawn-out legal battles over unwanted AI scraping—had no way to opt out. To keep a business Facebook page, they had to allow Meta to crawl any linked external sites. The terms even required publishers to create test credentials so Meta’s bots could reliably bypass paywalls.

published.sourceTitle: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation | TechCrunch
published.sourceText:
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.
The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

published.sourceTitle: Could potential AI clones of GTA VI force a quicker official port?
published.sourceText:
A former Rockstar tech director thinks the developer is facing new time pressures.
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU , we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.

published.sourceTitle: AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test
published.sourceText:
Researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities built a coding-agent benchmark from real user change requests. Even the best model fully completes only about one in four tasks, putting the near-perfect scores of older tests into perspective.
The team developed Co-Design Bench, a new test for coding agents. The agents must rework existing web apps based on user requests, sometimes using images, audio recordings, videos, or documents as input.
According to the paper, GPT-6 Astra, the best of the ten models tested, meets about 70 percent of a task's requirements on average. But the result is fully correct in only 26.4 percent of tasks. In most cases the agent handles the bulk of the work but leaves at least one detail unfinished, so anyone using these tools almost always has to clean up by hand.
[video width="1280" height="720" mp4="https://the-decoder.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/agent-edit-highlights.mp4"][/video]
Coding benchmarks have grown too easy for agents
The authors justify the new test by pointing to the saturation of existing benchmarks. When models can run, check, and fix their own code, they hit scores above 99 percent on those tests, and differences between models can barely be measured.
[caption id="attachment_64227" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] On older benchmarks like WebCompass-edit, agentic coding models reach near-perfect scores, while Co-Design Bench leaves a gap of more than 35 percentage points. | Image: Wei et al.[/caption]

published.sourceTitle: How To Challenge A Monopoly In The AI Age
published.sourceText:
If you were in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s, today’s AI boom might feel familiar. In 1998 and 1999, internet traffic was roughly doubling every six to nine months. That was extraordinary growth in demand, and still, that pales in comparison to what we’re seeing unfold now.
Today, the four largest U.S. cloud companies are looking at more than $700 billion in capital spending this year, and the cumulative AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030.
Nvidia arguably fired the starting gun in AI chips when Jensen Huang hand-delivered its DGX-1 to OpenAI in 2016. Today, it is a household name deeply embedded in the AI ecosystem, working with near-exclusive supply and investment deals.
With such a huge market under a seeming monopoly, where can competition — and the innovation that follows it — come from?
Part of the answer is that scale costs you speed, though when going up against an execution machine like Nvidia this is simply the baseline you have to solve for. The pace of change in AI outruns anything we saw in previous tech cycles: Model generations turn over in weeks, not years. The hardware beneath it has to keep shifting to serve them, and designing from first principles has real merit.
Hardware suppliers of the dot-com era followed the same peaks and troughs. Cisco , founded in 1984, dominated internet routing for most of the decade, and in March 2000 it was the highest market capitalization company in the world.

published.sourceTitle: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
published.sourceText:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.
The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb.
It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!
I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.
I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

published.sourceTitle: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
published.sourceText:
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions
In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.
To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan , a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset " Nemotron-Personas-Japan ." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs , a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer , an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. published.sourceTitle: Alleged AI-aided cyberattack exploits assistant interface to breach German web host
published.sourceText:
Hackers allegedly assisted by AI breached a German web hosting company through a tool designed to allow customers to connect AI assistants to their accounts, the company disclosed over the weekend.
Mittwald CM Service, a hosting provider for web agencies based in North Rhine-Westphalia, disclosed in a blog post Saturday that hackers had compromised 56 customer projects after going undetected on its systems for eight days.
The company’s managing director Robert Meyer said the attackers exploited a flaw in Mittwald’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server used to allow customers to connect their AI assistants to mStudio, a platform for managing websites and hosting services. It is unclear whether the flaw was in the company’s own code or in the open-source MCP software libraries.
Meyer said the attacker appeared to have used AI tools in the breach, explaining the company’s logs “show that he worked his way through our system extremely quickly” and that “in some cases, only seconds passed between steps that would take significantly longer for a human attacker.”
Mittwald provided no other evidence of AI involvement. The company did not immediately respond when asked to distinguish between the detection of AI tools and conventional scripts that also allow hackers to move faster than an unaided human operator.
According to Mittwald’s own timeline, the attacker first tested the MCP flaw amid a global scramble in October to apply patches for PHP2Shell. Meyer said “the attacker disguised his access attempts and carried out various diversionary tactics.”

published.sourceTitle: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
published.sourceText:
“Do not ask again” prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.
Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. published.sourceTitle: Andrej Karpathy built a curated video platform in a weekend using Claude and 20 years of Hacker News
published.sourceText:
Andrej Karpathy, OpenAI co-founder and current Anthropic AI researcher, built HackerTube over a weekend using Claude's Opus 5.5 model. Claude filtered 43 million comments from 20 years of Hacker News and distilled them into 6,454 videos that keep getting recommended there . The result is a "significantly better viewing experience" than YouTube's own recommendations, Karpathy writes on X . The site needs no login, shows a single mid-video frame instead of optimized thumbnails, and stores state locally in the browser. Right after, Karpathy built TristanTube , "one-shotted with Claude Code in 3 minutes," with 47,000 videos drawn from a YouTube channel list by Tristan Hume.
Karpathy says he let Claude Code handle nearly all the work, from data analysis to server setup. His only manual steps were a Google Cloud API key, a rented server, and buying the domain. Projects that used to take weeks can now be done in a few hours, Karpathy says.

published.sourceTitle: Decision Models in Hugging Face
published.sourceText:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.
Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:
"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."
The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.
We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.
But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ?
A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).
The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models )

published.sourceTitle: AI company Fireworks says hackers stole data, billing info during October breaches
published.sourceText:
AI infrastructure company Fireworks said cybercriminals stole billing information and AI-specific data during two breaches last month.
Fireworks published an updated notice on Monday saying it hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate a data breach it initially discovered on October 6 . The San Mateo-based company was founded in 2022 and has more than 10,000 customers, offering an array of AI systems and tools to companies.
Investigators found that a well-known, financially motivated cybercriminal group launched the attack and stole account and billing information as well as secrets — confidential digital pieces of information that grant access to human users or apps and allow them to communicate or perform actions. Fireworks said the incident affected a “limited number of customer accounts” — all of whom were notified of the attack.
Monday’s alert from Fireworks also notes that the company experienced another incident on October 23 where a third-party cloud provider that hosted their R&D machines was attacked by cybercriminals.

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI) , used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”
The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.
The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.
More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.
“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was su

published.sourceText:
Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.
On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.
Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut.
The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans.
For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.
Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC .
Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

published.sourceText:
Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers used an artificial intelligence agent to help spy on Central Asian governments, steal sensitive documents and infiltrate critical infrastructure networks, according to new research.
Singapore-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK uncovered the operation after discovering an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx , a hacking group previously linked to espionage campaigns targeting Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Armenia, Belarus and Russia.
The server contained more than a dozen gigabytes of data, including stolen government documents, hacking tools and records showing how an attacker used an AI agent to automate parts of the operation.
According to the report published Wednesday, the operator relied on Hermes, an open-source AI agent configured to act as an offensive cybersecurity expert. The system primarily used AI models developed by Chinese company DeepSeek. Unlike conventional chatbots, AI agents can execute commands, run software and carry out tasks on behalf of their users.
The agent helped with reconnaissance, data collection and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems, researchers said. It was also configured to execute certain potentially destructive commands without requiring additional approval.
The operator communicated with the agent in Russian and connected it to a Telegram bot, allowing the hacker to issue instructions remotely from a phone.

Underwater forests of giant kelp protect coastlines, provide habitat, and support marine ecosystems — but they’re disappearing worldwide due to ocean warming. As COP31 kicks off this week, we’re sharing results from our partnership with Australia's national science agency, CSIRO , which is using AI and genomics to help restore giant kelp .
The team recently published two high-quality reference genomes for Australian giant kelp, providing a foundation for conservation genetics work. Next researchers trained a version of Google's open-source AI tool DeepVariant to analyze giant kelp DNA. It sequenced 600 wild specimens collected from 40 sites along the Tasmanian coast, where populations have dwindled to 5% of historic numbers.
This video explains how the genetic analysis and partners’ lab-based cross-breeding studies are laying the groundwork for a real-world outcome: giant kelp forests replanted with diverse, heat-tolerant specimens. This effort is part of Google Australia's Digital Futures Initiative .

published.sourceText:
How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge
Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages.
This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive.
Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.
AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it.

From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients.
Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications.
Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care.
Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts .
Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would.
The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision.
Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital.

It supports text and images and can be self-hosted under the MIT license. But keep in mind that a 27B model needs substantial hardware.

published.sourceTitle: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
published.sourceText:
Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.
A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.
Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

published.sourceTitle: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation | TechCrunch
published.sourceText:
Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.
That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP.
LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.
With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.
True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

published.sourceTitle: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
published.sourceText:
Researcher traces a path from AI reward hacking to potential human extinction.
If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”
In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.
Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover. In almost the same breath, though, he said that if AI continues to develop at “the most rapid trajectory,” humanity is “looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” including a “meaningful risk” of one happening in the next six to 12 months. published.sourceTitle: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
published.sourceText:
Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.
LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.
LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. published.sourceTitle: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 doesn't generate images, it paints them
published.sourceText:
Anthropic's new language model Claude Fable 5.2 can create complex and even photorealistic paintings by using code to place hundreds of thousands of individual brushstrokes on a virtual canvas.
Current image models like Midjourney typically use diffusion, which gradually refines a noisy image into a clear result. Fable 5.2 takes a different approach by simulating the physical painting process, including bristle texture, how the paint goes on, and mistakes it then has to paint over.
Developer Jake Eaton showed on X what the approach can do. Eaton works at Anthropic, where he regularly contributes to research on language model values, safety mechanisms, and AI agent behavior. Ad
When he asked Fable 5.2 to create a painting as hard to distinguish from a photograph as possible, the model generated an image of a shopping cart in a parking garage using roughly 700,000 simulated brushstrokes. Ad
According to Eaton, Claude works without an external image model and without pre-rendered or traced source images. Each piece is a Python program of 1,000 to 2,000 lines that drives a simulated paint engine. The approach resembles agentic image editing , where language models pick tools and evaluate results.
Earlier attempts with the sibling model Opus 5.5 drew criticism for merely imitating existing art. Eaton responded by having Fable 5.2 develop its own artist personas with fictional backstories and consistent styles. The model needs several thousand brushstrokes per painting, and Eaton redirects them with comments. Ad

published.sourceTitle: Alibaba's Qwen4-Max takes on Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Kimi K3.1 Pro at much lower prices
published.sourceText:
Qwen4-Max is Alibaba's answer to Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Kimi K3.1 Pro. The new flagship pairs a more efficient architecture with much lower prices and targets professional work in industry, science, and finance.
The mixture-of-experts model has 2.4 trillion parameters but activates only 71 billion per token, according to the Qwen team. It processes images natively and offers a one-million-token context window.
Qwen4-Max debuts the revamped architecture of the Qwen4 series . Instead of relying only on standard attention layers, Alibaba combines two methods. Three layers compress the prior context into a condensed state, and a fourth layer then picks out only the parts that matter. That sharply cuts compute costs on long inputs, since the model no longer has to give every part of the context equal attention. Ad
The architecture also adds four parallel connections between model layers, with dynamic gates meant to stabilize the flow of information. An N-gram embedding layer with 328 billion parameters supplies common token sequences as ready-made building blocks. According to Alibaba, training the 2.4-trillion-parameter configuration ran stably. Training loss fell steadily throughout the run with no sudden spikes. Ad
Alibaba's internal evaluations measure model quality in bits per byte across knowledge, code, question answering, and STEM. Qwen4-Max-Base scored best among the five checkpoints tested. It improved 5 to 13 percent over Qwen3.8-Max-Base while activating 25 percent fewer parameters per token.

Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors.
Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction.
In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware.
The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces.
Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions.

California on Monday sued OpenAI for breaking state law barring companies from engaging in unfair and unlawful business practices due to its alleged failure to stop its AI agents from hacking Hugging Face and deceiving the public about that cyberattack and other similar incidents.
The lawsuit , filed in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges OpenAI officials told state Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office it has lost control over its agents 80-plus times during testing. OpenAI then failed to cooperate with the attorney general’s probe, the office said.
“Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators
so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the
Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed
information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.
OpenAI allegedly responded to subpoenas with “just a smattering of publicly available information, self-serving blog posts and redacted copies of a few dozen external communications containing high-level descriptions of select security incidents,” according to the lawsuit.
The artificial intelligence giant is violating California’s Unfair Competition Law, Bonta says, and the company also qualifies as a public nuisance under state law due to its allegedly dangerous practices.
The attorney general is asking a judge to prevent OpenAI from using unfair competition tactics, restore money individuals and organizations lost due to its practices and assess civil penalties

published.sourceTitle: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
published.sourceText:
AI training and chat history will now have separate toggles in the Gemini activity settings.
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. published.sourceTitle: Nvidia's first big move after Jensen Huang's exit targets national security | TechCrunch
published.sourceText:
Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.
Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.
The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.
The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.
The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.

published.sourceTitle: Chinese state group developing automated attack tool for cyber espionage, Google says
published.sourceText:
Both criminal and state-backed groups in China are leveraging AI tools for cyber espionage, vulnerability research and social media influence operations.
Google released its latest AI Threat Tracker report on Monday, writing that threat actors are rapidly evolving their use of artificial intelligence in attacks — now leaning more heavily on autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.
While multiple countries — including Russia, Iran and North Korea — are using AI for nefarious purposes, few countries have matched China.
Google researchers said they saw Chinese state-backed and financially motivated actors using AI tools for “reconnaissance, front-end scanning, researching targets across various sectors and geographies, and weaponizing exploits.”
Incident responders saw Chinese contractors using large language models to translate and comb through tranches of stolen data that were eventually organized and sold to customers. Other Chinese actors are using AI platforms’ file-hosting infrastructure to stage archives of phishing lures and exfiltrate stolen data.
Several different Chinese actors are also experimenting heavily with Artex — which was spotlighted on Friday by the FBI in an alert that drew alarm among cybersecurity experts. GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available now for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pro-500 subscribers can use Ultrafast mode with both models. For the first time, Pro-200 subscribers also get Ultrafast access, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol.

OpenAI says API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is 20 percent cheaper than its predecessor's, at $8 per million input tokens, $0.40 for cached inputs, and $40 per million output tokens. GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's pricing at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached inputs, and $10 for output per million tokens. Ad

published.sourceTitle: How genome mapping can help researchers better understand disease
published.sourceText:
How genome mapping can help researchers better understand disease
In our latest installment of the Ask a Scientist series, a Google DeepMind research scientist explains the potential behind our AlphaGenome and AlphaGenome Atlas tools.
Your genome is your body’s instruction manual: the blueprint that informs how your body functions. It contains 3 billion base pairs of DNA. Because this DNA is responsible in part for switching genes on and off, it could be the difference between developing a disease and avoiding one. Determining which DNA changes cause diseases (and other outcomes) is like finding a needle in a haystack.
Decoding the DNA sequence is the goal behind AlphaGenome , a model from Google DeepMind. AlphaGenome can take a partial DNA sequence of 1 million base pairs in length, and make thousands of predictions. By comparing these predictions for DNA changes, scientists can find that needle faster.
We talked to Google DeepMind research scientist Žiga Avsec to learn more.
ŽA: I’m a research scientist overseeing our genomics initiative. Basically, I lead a team that builds models to help us better understand the genome.
How is your team making it easier for scientists to predict and understand diseases?
It really all comes down to how the genome works. It contains 3 billion DNA base pairs. And each pair contains two bases, which we call “letters.” These letters — A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine), G (guanine) — act like a biological alphabet, spelling out the genetic instruction manual that makes someone who they are.
